title: Why You Forget Why You Walked Into a Room
desc: You walk into the kitchen with a clear plan, and the moment you step through the door, it's gone. It's not your age and it's not a bad memory. Psychologists call it the doorway effect. In this video we look at the experiments that discovered it, why your brain files life into chapters, and simple ways to stop doorways from stealing your thoughts.
sources: Radvansky, Krawietz & Tamplin (2011). Walking through doorways causes forgetting: Further explorations. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.
Radvansky & Copeland (2006). Walking through doorways causes forgetting: Situation models and experienced space. Memory & Cognition.
Zacks, Speer, Swallow, Braver & Reynolds (2007). Event perception: A mind-brain perspective. Psychological Bulletin.
University of Notre Dame news release (2011): Walking through doorways causes forgetting, new research shows.

segments.say: You're on the couch. You think, I need to grab something from the kitchen. You get up, you walk over, you step through the door...
...and it's gone. You're standing in the kitchen, staring at the fridge, with absolutely no idea why you're there.
You walk back to the couch, sit down, and of course, you remember instantly. Classic.
This happens to almost everyone, and it's not because your memory is bad. Scientists have actually tested it, and the surprising answer is that the door itself might be part of the problem.

In this video, we'll look at the experiments that discovered the doorway effect, why your brain splits your life into chapters, a strange twist in the results, and some easy ways to stop doorways from stealing your thoughts. And stick around for part three, because the researchers also tested the obvious fix, going back to the room, and the result is not what you'd expect.
Part one. The doorway experiments.
Most of us blame age, stress or a bad night of sleep. And those things can matter. But the doorway effect also shows up in young, well rested students in a lab. So something else is going on.

show.sub: It happens to rested students too.

segments.say: The researcher behind this is psychologist Gabriel Radvansky at the University of Notre Dame. He and his colleagues wanted to know if walking through a doorway really makes people forget, or if it just feels that way.

show.what: Does walking through a doorway actually make people forget? They tested it in virtual and real rooms.

segments.say: In the first experiments, students played a simple video game. They walked through virtual rooms, picked up an object from a table, and carried it to another table. Sometimes the next table was in the same room. Sometimes it was through a doorway, in a new room. And the distance walked was kept the same.

show.title: Experiment 1: virtual rooms
items: Same room, or through a door

segments.say: Along the way, the game asked them what they were carrying. And the result was clear. People who had just walked through a doorway forgot more often than people who walked the same distance in a single room.

show.title: The result
items: Through a doorway: forgot more often

segments.say: Then the researchers took it out of the screen and into real rooms. Students carried real objects in a box, walking either across one room or the same distance through a doorway. Same result. Doorways caused more forgetting.

show.title: Experiment 2: real rooms
items: Across one room, or through a door

segments.say: What makes these experiments clever is how boring they are. Same objects, same distances, same kind of people. The only real difference was whether there was a doorway. So when memory got worse, the doorway was the main suspect.
So the doorway effect is real. But why would a door, which is basically just a hole in a wall, mess with your memory?
Part two. Your brain thinks in chapters.

Your brain doesn't record life like one long, endless video. It cuts it into chunks. Episodes. Making breakfast. Walking to the bus. Talking to a friend. Psychologists call the moments between those chunks event boundaries.

This idea comes from what's called event segmentation theory, developed by psychologist Jeffrey Zacks and colleagues. When something important in your situation changes, your brain closes the old chapter and opens a new one.

show.what: The brain splits experience into events, and updates its model of the situation at the boundaries.

segments.say: It's the same reason books have chapters and movies cut between scenes. Storytellers didn't invent that structure out of nowhere. They're working with how our brains already like to organize experience.

And it's not just doors. In this research, event boundaries tend to show up whenever something important in the situation changes. A new place. A new goal. Someone new walking in. In studies where people watch films, viewers tend to agree on where one event ends and the next begins, and the brain responds at those moments.

show.title: Other event boundaries
items: A scene change in a film

segments.say: And a doorway is a perfect event boundary. New room, new lighting, new objects, new possibilities. Your brain goes, okay, new scene. And it files the old scene away, along with the thought you were carrying.
The thought isn't deleted. It's just in the previous chapter, and the page has turned. That's why going back to the couch can bring it back. You're standing in that old scene again.

There's a name for the kind of memory the doorway attacks. Prospective memory. That's remembering to do something in the future, like grabbing the scissors or taking your medicine. It's fragile, because usually nothing around you is reminding you of it. You have to carry it yourself.
It also makes sense that this happens more when you're juggling a lot. A thought you're only half holding is easier to drop when the page turns.

You probably know a modern version of this too. You unlock your phone to check one thing, you see a notification, and suddenly, what was it again? Switching apps can feel a lot like walking through a door. That one hasn't been tested the same way as the doorway studies, but it fits the same idea. New screen, new chapter.
Quick question. What's the strangest thing you've walked into a room for, and completely forgotten? Let me know in the comments.
So, new room, new chapter. That seems simple. But the researchers found something in the next experiment that doesn't fit that simple story at all.
Part three. The strange twist.
If the problem is being in a different room than where you made the memory, then going back to the original room should fix it. Right? The researchers tested that too.

In a third experiment, people walked through several doorways and ended up back in the very same room where they started. And their memory did not get better. Just passing through doorways was enough to cause the forgetting, even when they returned to the original room.

show.title: Experiment 3: the twist
items: End up back in the starting room

segments.say: So it's not only about where you are. It's about the act of crossing the boundary. Each door is like hitting a save and close button on what you were just thinking.

One explanation the researchers offered is about competition. After a boundary, your brain is now holding more than one chapter, the old one and the new one. When you try to remember, those chapters compete with each other, and the thing you wanted gets harder to find.

show.title: Why crossing makes it worse
items: They compete when you try to remember

segments.say: And that's why the couch trick only works sometimes. When it works, it's usually because something on the couch, the TV, your phone, the conversation, reminds you of the thought. Not because you magically returned to the right room.

show.sub: works because of cues, not magic

segments.say: Here's the part that should make you feel better. This is a sign of a healthy brain. Splitting life into chapters is how you remember things in order, understand stories, and keep track of what's happening. The doorway glitch is just the price you pay for a very good filing system.
Part four. How to beat the doorway.

You can't remove the doors from your house. Well, you can, but please don't. Here's what you can do instead. These tricks are simple, and they work for the same reason. They keep the thought active, or they give it an anchor that survives the boundary.
One. Say it out loud. Before you get up, say the thing. Scissors. Charger. Water. Hearing it makes it a stronger memory, and a single word is easy to carry through a door.

show.title: 1. Say it out loud
items: One word is easy to carry

segments.say: Two. Keep repeating it while you walk. It feels silly, but you're keeping the thought active, so there's nothing to file away when you cross the boundary.
Three. Make a picture. Imagine the thing in a silly way. A giant phone charger stuck in the fridge. Weird images are easier to remember than plain words.

show.title: 3. Make it a weird picture
items: Imagine it in a silly way
A giant charger in the fridge

segments.say: Here's another one. Finish the thought before you move. Instead of a vague feeling of needing something, say a complete sentence in your head. I'm going to the kitchen to get scissors for this box. A clear sentence is much harder to lose than a fuzzy idea.

And four. If you still forget, don't panic. Stand still for a moment and think about what you were doing just before you got up. You're not searching for the item. You're searching for the chapter. Very often, the item comes right back with it.

show.title: 4. Search for the chapter
items: The thought often comes back with it

segments.say: And five. Carry a clue. If the thing you need goes with an object, take that object with you. Going to get batteries for the remote? Bring the remote. It's a physical reminder that walks through the door with you.

show.title: 5. Carry a clue
items: The reminder walks through the door too

segments.say: One important note. Walking into a room and forgetting why is normal, and it happens at every age. But if forgetting is getting a lot worse over time, or it's starting to get in the way of daily life, that's worth talking to a doctor about. Occasional doorway moments are just your brain's filing system at work.

show.sub: Big changes? Talk to a doctor.

segments.say: Quick recap. Doors are event boundaries. When you cross one, your brain closes the old chapter, and the thought you were carrying gets filed away with it. Going back doesn't always fix it. But saying it, repeating it, picturing it, or carrying a clue makes it much harder to lose.

show.title: Quick recap
items: Your brain closes the old chapter
Say it, repeat it, picture it, carry it

segments.say: So the next time you're standing in the kitchen, staring at the fridge, wondering why you're there, don't blame your memory. Blame the door. Your brain just turned the page a little too quickly.
Honestly, there's something kind of nice about it. Your brain is constantly turning your life into a story, one scene at a time. Sometimes it just turns the page before you're done reading.
